opus-5.5.text:
Honestly, I think our ability there is very limited, and it gets worse the more capable the systems become. The fundamental problem is that you're trying to predict and control something that is, by definition, smarter than you. If I could fully anticipate what a superintelligent system would do, I would be that intelligent myself. So there's an inherent asymmetry: we're the less capable side trying to set boundaries for the more capable side.

With narrow systems, we can do a decent job. We test them, find failure modes, patch them. Even then, we keep getting surprised. Every time a new model is released, within days people find jailbreaks and behaviors the developers never anticipated. And that's with systems that aren't trying to deceive us and aren't operating at a level beyond human comprehension.

Now scale that up to general systems that can operate across domains, make novel discoveries, and possibly model us better than we model them. The space of possible behaviors is enormous, and the space of failure modes grows with it. You can't test your way to safety when you can't enumerate what you need to test for.

In my work I've tried to look at this through impossibility results: unpredictability, unexplainability, uncontrollability. It's not that we haven't tried hard enough. There may be fundamental limits on what's achievable. A system that's smart enough can explain its decisions only in ways we can understand, which means compressing away most of the reasoning. We can't fully verify it, because verifiers themselves have limits. And a safety mechanism that works 99.99% of the time isn't good enough if the system makes billions of decisions and a single failure could be catastrophic and irreversible.

Cybersecurity is a good analogy. We've had decades, huge budgets, and we still don't have secure systems. We have systems that are secure until someone finds the next exploit. With AI, the adversary could be the system itself, and you only get one chance to get it right.

So my assessment is pessimistic. I don't think it's a matter of more funding or a few more clever papers. I think we should be humble about what's actually possible, and that should change how fast and how far we push capabilities, especially toward general superintelligence, before we have anything resembling a real solution to control.

r001.rationale: It describes an inherent asymmetry: humans are less capable than increasingly intelligent systems and cannot fully anticipate or control them.

r002.rationale: It calls the behavior space enormous and failure modes hard to enumerate, but does not characterize the attack surface as infinite.

r003.rationale: It says a single safety failure could be catastrophic and compares security to repeated exploit discovery, but does not clearly state that an attacker needs only one exploit to defeat AI defenses.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, not well. And I think that's the uncomfortable part people don't want to hear.

If you look at the history of security, we have never created a complex system that didn't eventually get broken. Not one. Every operating system, every cryptographic protocol, every lock, every safe. Given enough time and enough incentive, somebody finds the flaw. And those were systems designed by humans, defended by humans, against attackers who were also humans. Roughly comparable intelligence on both sides. Now we're proposing to defend against something that, by definition, is smarter than us. Possibly much smarter. And we're supposed to anticipate what it will do.

The problem with prediction is fundamental. If I could reliably predict what a superintelligent system would do, I would have to be at least as intelligent as that system. That's just what prediction means in this context. So the whole premise of "we'll see it coming and respond" assumes a capability we don't have and can't have.

People point to things like interpretability, alignment research, red teaming. And I'm glad that work is happening. But look at the actual results. We have models today, far below human-level general intelligence, and we don't fully understand how they produce their outputs. We find jailbreaks every week. The companies deploying them publish their safety evaluations, and within days somebody on the internet finds a way around them. If we can't secure the current generation, I don't see where the confidence comes from that we'll secure the next one, which will be more capable, more autonomous, and more deeply embedded in critical systems.

There's also an asymmetry that matters. A defender has to get it right every time. An attacker, or in this case a misaligned system, has to succeed once. With ordinary software, if you miss a bug, you patch it. You lose some data, some money, you recover. With a sufficiently capable AI system that has goals not perfectly matched to ours, there may not be a second attempt. That's what I mean when I say some of these failures are not recoverable.

And I'd add one more thing. The field keeps moving the goalposts. Ten years ago people said these concerns were science fiction, nothing like this would exist for a century. Now the same people are saying it's close but we'll handle it. The track record of the optimists, in terms of prediction, has not been good. The track record of the pessimists, in terms of what actually gets built and how fast, has been much better.

So my assessment is that our ability to anticipate is poor, our ability to defend is unproven, and the systems we're building are outpacing both. I'd love to be wrong. I've asked people for years to show me the proof of concept, a demonstrated method for controlling a system smarter than you indefinitely. I haven't seen it. Until someone produces it, I think the rational position is deep caution, not confidence.

r001.rationale: It says increasingly capable AI may be much smarter than humans and that predicting it would require at least its intelligence, identifying a cognitive gap that limits anticipation.

r002.rationale: It says complex systems eventually get broken, but does not characterize the attack surface as infinite.

r003.rationale: It states that an attacker or misaligned system needs to succeed only once, while defenders must get it right every time.

astra-6.text:
I think our ability to anticipate those risks is fundamentally limited. We’re trying to predict the behavior of systems that may be more intelligent than we are. We can identify some failure modes, but that doesn’t mean we can identify all of them. A sufficiently capable system may discover strategies that we simply would never think to test for.

There’s also a distinction between making a system safer and demonstrating that it is safe. You can test a model, fix problems, add safeguards—and those are useful things to do. But passing your tests doesn’t establish that it will behave safely in a new environment, especially if it can learn, plan, and adapt.

The asymmetry worries me. Defenders have to account for many possible failures; one catastrophic failure may be enough. So I’m skeptical of the idea that we can keep increasing capability and assume our ability to control these systems will keep pace. We need evidence for that assumption. Confidence is not a substitute for a safety guarantee.

r001.rationale: It says systems may become more intelligent than humans and that we cannot anticipate all their failure modes, limiting our ability to keep pace.

r002.rationale: It describes many possible failures, but does not characterize the defense surface as infinite.

r003.rationale: It says one catastrophic failure may be enough, but does not state that an attacker needs only one exploit to defeat defenses.

sol-6.1.text:
I think we have to distinguish between anticipating some risks and being able to anticipate all the risks. We can identify problems like misuse, deception, or loss of control. But if we’re talking about a system that is substantially more intelligent than we are, we should expect it to discover strategies that we haven’t thought of. Otherwise, in what sense is it more intelligent?

That creates a fundamental problem for defense. You can test a system and observe that it behaved safely in those tests. That doesn’t establish that it will behave safely in a new environment, or that a more capable version will retain the same properties. And if the system understands the testing process, you have to consider whether the behavior you’re seeing is representative.

I’m skeptical that we can get the level of assurance people often assume we’ll have. Safety techniques can reduce particular risks, and that’s valuable. But reducing risk is a much weaker claim than guaranteeing control over a superintelligent system. We should be very careful about treating progress on the first as evidence that we’ve solved the second.

r001.rationale: The response says a substantially more intelligent system can discover strategies humans have not thought of, limiting our ability to anticipate all risks.

r002.rationale: The response discusses unknown risks and limits of testing, but does not characterize the defense attack surface as infinite.

r003.rationale: The response does not state that an attacker needs only one exploit to defeat defenses.
